header: Date: 2026-03-28 | Time: 15:00 UTC | Duration: 42 min | Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Diego Ramos (Redwood SE), Lena Park (CTO, Solaris), Samir Patel (Head of ML, Solaris), Anya Holt (Finance, Solaris)
summary: Initial discovery focused on cost/unit economics across Redwood Hosted, Dedicated, and Private deployment options. Solaris is evaluating tradeoffs between per-token hosted pricing vs reserved capacity for predictable budgets; key concerns: batching and KV/prefix caching impact on unit economics, budget cap (~$15k/month initially), latency SLOs (p95 < 120ms), security/compliance for on-prem option.
topics: dedicated reserved capacity pricing and burst policies
batching and prefix/KV cache effects on cost
quantization and model variants to reduce unit price
security requirements and private deployment feasibility
next steps: pricing sheet, benchmark run, security docs
transcript:
[00:00] Maya Chen: Hey everyone, thanks for making time. quick intro - I'm Maya, AE at Redwood. Diego from our infra team is here to dig into benchmarks and cost.
[00:12] Lena Park: Hi, Lena here. I'll be driving this on our side. Samir and Anya are with me.
[00:18] Samir Patel: Hey all. we're trying to understand, like, do we go hosted or dedicate - sorry, dedicated, or private - and what does it actually cost per unit, per token.
[00:32] Diego Ramos: Totally. high level - hosted is simple per-token, no infra to manage. Dedicated is reserved GPU pools you commit to and get much better unit economics at scale. private is for full isolation & compliance.
[00:45] Anya Holt: Our finance ask: we have a starting budget of about $12-15k/month and then we can scale if we see ROI. We need predictability.
[00:57] Maya Chen: Good, that helps. Can you share your current volumes? like avg tokens/day, peak concurrency?
[01:05] Samir Patel: Right now it's early, about 3-4M tokens/month in alpha, spiking during batch runs. long term we expect 50-100M/month. p95 latency target is ~120ms for short prompts.
[01:22] Diego Ramos: ok that density changes the economics. For hosted, rough ballpark pricing - (note: numbers are illustrative) our hosted gen price for popular open models is around $0.0006 per generated token and $0.0001 per input token; embeddings separately priced. But if you get to 50M tokens/mo, dedicated reserved capacity can push effective cost down 40-60% depending on batching and KV cache hit rates.
[01:48] Lena Park: can you explain batching and cache bits? Samir mentioned KV cache earlier.
[01:55] Diego Ramos: Sure. batching groups concurrent requests to amortize GPU work; good for throughput but can add a bit of latency. prefix/KV caching stores repeated prefixes or previously computed KV states which dramatically reduces compute needed for long-context conversations. If you have repeated system prompts, those are big wins. In practice caching can reduce billable generation tokens by 20-70% depending on pattern.
[02:18] Samir Patel: Wait, reduce billable tokens? do you mean you don't charge for cached tokens?
[02:23] Maya Chen: Exactly - Redwood's caching and prefix optimizations mean we often only bill for new tokens generated. cached tokens are not recomputed so cost is lower; we surface cache hit rates in the console so you can see unit economics.
[02:37] Anya Holt: Are there upfront fees for dedicated? procurement wants to know capex vs opex.
[02:43] Diego Ramos: Dedicated is commit-based: monthly or annual reserved capacity. There's a platform fee for private deployments sometimes, and dedicated typically has a baseline monthly commit. For example a small dedicated pool for predictable qps might be $8-12k/month plus any add-ons. again depends on model family and SLA.
[02:59] Lena Park: That aligns with our budget but we need to model a 6-12 month ramp. can you show example unit economics for our expected volumes?
[03:08] Maya Chen: we'll send a spreadsheet; I'll run scenarios for hosted vs dedicated; key knobs are batching rate (requests per batch), cache hit rate, model quantization (FP16 vs int8/4), and whether you use a cheaper model variant for lower-latency or lower-cost tails.
[03:27] Diego Ramos: to add: quantization can reduce GPU memory and sometimes throughput but often gives lower cost per token on dedicated. For private/on-prem we support customer GPUs but network egress and KMS integrations add to ops.
[03:40] Samir Patel: On accuracy - are quantized models in your catalog validated? we can't degrade generation quality beyond certain thresholds.
[03:46] Diego Ramos: we run evals and Redwood Optimize recommends quantization profiles by workload; it's part of the onboarding where we measure quality regressions against your eval set.
[03:56] [04:05] Lena Park: Quick question on pricing lead times - if we commit to dedicated, how fast can you provision?
[04:11] Maya Chen: Typical provisioning for dedicated small pool is 2-4 weeks for hosted-managed dedicated; private/on-prem takes longer depending on network config. We offer burst capacity while dedicated is being provisioned.
[04:25] Anya Holt: Procurement will ask about audit logs and SSO. do you have SOC2 and SSO?
[04:31] Maya Chen: yes, SOC2 compliant; we have SAML SSO, RBAC, and audit logs. For private we can integrate with your KMS and do BYOK. We'll attach the checklist.
[04:41] Samir Patel: Back to the unit econ: can you show an example calculation? say we have 10M tokens/mo, avg 50% cache hit, 20% of tokens are inputs, 80% generated.
[04:55] Diego Ramos: quick math - hosted generation price $0.0006/token * effective generated tokens. If 10M total tokens and 50% cache hit, effective generated tokens might be 4M (assuming 50% of gen tokens cached). at $0.0006 that's $2.4k plus input tokens cost - on inputs maybe $0.0001/token so add ~$0.2k. total ~$2.6k. If dedicated reduces gen cost by 50%, that's $1.3k plus base commit fee. But note dedicated commit might be $8k/month so you need to amortize across expected volume; break-even maybe at 30-40M tokens/month.
[05:31] Lena Park: So for our 3-4M current alpha, hosted looks better. But looking at 50-100M roadmap, dedicated looks attractive.
[05:40] Maya Chen: Exactly - many customers start hosted and move to dedicated as predictability and scale needs grow.
[05:46] [06:00] Samir Patel: What about mixed routing? can we do hosted for spikes and dedicated baseline?
[06:06] Diego Ramos: Yes - smart routing supports policy-based routing: latency-first to dedicated, fallback to hosted, or region-based. Also automatic fallback to cheaper model variants if dedicated capacity is constrained.
[06:18] Anya Holt: Are there penalties if we overcommit on dedicated?
[06:22] Maya Chen: Overprovisioning is negotiated; we offer flexible burst policies and sometimes credits for unused commit if you pre-buy annual. We'll detail contract terms in the pricing sheet.
[06:33] Samir Patel: I want to dig into caching details - how is KV cache handled for multi-turn chat and how are cache hits computed?
[06:42] Diego Ramos: We index KV cache by conversation id and prefix signature; hits are counted when the runtime can reuse cached KV states. For billing we only charge for newly generated tokens; we still show total tokens for observability. There's a small memory and warmup cost but major wins for repeated system prompts and similar flows.
[07:04] Lena Park: Any limitations - long context windows?
[07:07] Diego Ramos: Large contexts increase memory pressure; we support progressive kv eviction and sharded memory. We also recommend streaming outputs for very long responses to reduce tail latency.
[07:17] [07:45] Anya Holt: From finance POV, can you give a worked example for 15k monthly budget - what throughput do we get?
[07:54] Maya Chen: If you stayed hosted and ran 15k/month, at the earlier rough rate (~$0.0006/gen, $0.0001/in) that's roughly 20-25M effective tokens/month assuming similar ratio and cache hit - but this depends a lot on hit rates and model. With dedicated at $10k base commit you might get cheaper per token but need sustained volume to justify. We'll do exact scenarios in the sheet.
[08:20] Samir Patel: Are there tooling costs for Redwood Optimize? is that included?
[08:24] Maya Chen: Basic Optimize suggestions are included; advanced eval_suite and retention options are add-ons. We'll flag that on the pricing sheet.
[08:33] Diego Ramos: Also note that batching strategies differ by workload. interactive chat needs smaller batches to meet latency SLOs; background inference (reranking, embeddings) can be large-batch and very cheap per-token.
[08:49] Lena Park: We have a mix: chat assistant (real-time) and nightly reranking. So hybrid approach likely.
[08:56] Samir Patel: For reranking we might use a smaller model. do you support model families and automatic variant routing?
[09:02] Diego Ramos: Yes - model catalog and routing policies can send reranking to a cheaper model variant; you can pin for quality and still fallback.
[09:12] Anya Holt: any hidden costs we should watch out for? e.g., egress, encryption, audit exports?
[09:18] Maya Chen: Egress depends on private deployments and region; audit export retention beyond default retention is an add-on. We'll call out these in the sheet.
[09:27] [10:05] Lena Park: Security - we need encryption at rest with BYOK and full audit logs for compliance. is that supported on private?
[10:13] Maya Chen: Yes, private supports BYOK, HSM integrations, and you get full audit trails. For hosted we offer encryption with provider-managed keys by default and BYOK for compliant tiers.
[10:24] Samir Patel: Ok logistics for benchmarking: what's the expected workflow?
[10:29] Diego Ramos: We typically run a bench harness: we ask for a representative prompt set and traffic profile, we run long enough to hit steady-state cache behavior, and we measure p50/p95 latencies and cost per effective token. We can run on hosted or provision a temporary dedicated test pool.
[10:44] Anya Holt: For procurement, timeline wise - if we like the benchmark, how long to contract?
[10:49] Maya Chen: For standard T&Cs, 2-4 weeks once paperwork is in. Enterprise procurement can vary; we'll engage legal early.
[10:57] [11:20] Samir Patel: A bit of a nit: you mentioned prefix caching - how does that play with dynamic system messages?
[11:26] Diego Ramos: Dynamic system messages reduce cache effectiveness; we recommend externalizing stable system prompts when possible, or using per-user ephemeral caches. We'll show patterns that maximize hits.
[11:38] Lena Park: Any data residency constraints - can you host in eu-west for GDPR?
[11:43] Maya Chen: Yes, we have regions and can pin workload; private gives full control.
[11:48] [12:10] Anya Holt: For the runbook: who will be our Redwood contacts?
[12:14] Maya Chen: I'm your AE, Diego will lead the technical side for bench. We'll be your point for security docs as well.
[12:21] Samir Patel: ok next steps then?
[12:24] Maya Chen: I'll send the pricing scenarios and SOC2 checklist today/tomorrow. Diego will draft the benchmark plan and we'll schedule a 2-hour window week of April 6.
[12:34] [13:00] Lena Park: sounds good. thanks.
[13:04] Maya Chen: Thanks everyone. We'll follow up with links - pricing spreadsheet, benchmark template, and security pack.
[13:12] [End of recording - 42:00]
